title: Find the commit that deleted a line nobody can explain
summary: A config key vanished and nobody remembers why. Use the pickaxe to search the content of every commit in history, not just the current files.
mental_model: `grep` searches the files you have. `log -S` searches every version of every file that ever existed, and reports the commits where the count of a string changed. It is the only tool that finds deletions.

steps.title: Confirm it is really gone
steps.why: Plain grep searches the working tree. It finds nothing, which proves only that the setting is not here *now* — not what happened to it.
steps.expect: Nothing for the circuit breaker; exit code 1 is a normal 'no matches'.

steps.title: Search every commit that ever existed
steps.why: `-S` is the pickaxe: it lists every commit where the number of occurrences of the string changed. Three come back — it was introduced in the config, used in the client, then removed from both. Scoping with `-- config.py` narrows it to the two that touched the setting itself.
steps.expect: Three commits unscoped, two when limited to config.py.

verify.label: the pickaxe found the add and the delete in config.py

steps.title: Read the commit that removed it
steps.why: Now you have a culprit and a message: 'Simplify retry handling'. The diff shows the deletion was collateral damage from an unrelated change — the exact thing nobody remembers doing.

steps.title: -S versus -G
steps.why: `-S` counts occurrences: it misses a commit that moved a line without changing the count. `-G` matches the diff text itself with a regex, so it catches modifications too. Use -G when -S comes back empty.
steps.expect: -G returns more commits, because it sees changes that kept the count the same.

steps.title: Follow a specific line through time
steps.why: `log -L` takes a line range and a file, and prints every commit that changed those lines with the patch. It is the most precise history tool git has.
steps.expect: Each commit that touched the first three lines, with the diff inline.

steps.title: Grep inside an old commit
steps.why: `git grep <pattern> <rev>` searches the tree of that commit, not your working files. Here the rev is the *parent* of the removal — written `<sha>^` — which is where the setting last existed.
steps.expect: The setting, found in the commit just before it was deleted.

steps.title: Restore what was lost
steps.why: The parent of the deleting commit is the last good state, so `<sha>^` is the source to restore from. That caret is the whole trick, and it works for any 'undo this one deletion' problem.

verify.label: the lost setting is back in the working tree
the deleted setting was found in history and restored
verify.hint: git log -S CIRCUIT_BREAKER_THRESHOLD finds the deleting commit; restore --source=<sha>^ brings it back

verify.label: the pickaxe still shows the add and the delete in config.py
history is intact — you searched it, you did not rewrite it
verify.hint: restoring a file is a working-tree change, not a history change

pitfalls: `-S` takes a string by default, not a regex. Add `--pickaxe-regex` if you need patterns.
`-S` finds only commits where the *count* changed. A line moved between files is invisible to it — reach for `-G`.
Both are slow on huge repositories. Narrow with `-- <path>` or `--since` when you can.
`git grep` searches the working tree; `git grep <rev>` searches that commit. Forgetting the rev is the most common mistake here.
cheatsheet: commits where the occurrence count changed
commits whose diff matches the pattern
…with the diffs, to read what happened
